column3: Repeats the arrival and fulfilment of a divine promise, supplying a close historical parallel to the focus's promised event.
Opens the Dhu al-Qarnayn account whose concluding declaration is the focus.
God's forgiveness and mercy offer only a broad resonance with the mercy attributed to the barrier.
Names mercy from the speaker's Lord amid a rejected warning, supporting the focus's attribution of mercy to the Lord.
The immediately preceding ayah establishes the barrier's effective protection that the focus calls a mercy and declares temporary.
The divine names establish mercy generally but add no event, barrier, or promise relation.
Its final-promise formula and gathering give a nearby parallel for the focus's future promise.
The community's request for a barrier against Gog and Magog directly supplies the danger to which the focus responds.
Uses the same dakk root for the crushing of earth and mountains, closely illuminating the barrier's future flattening.
Mentions the Lord's mercy but concerns human withholding rather than the barrier or promised event.
Dhu al-Qarnayn's provision of a protective redm is the construction the focus identifies as a mercy.
The repeated dakk description gives a direct lexical and eschatological parallel to the focus's dakkā'.
Mercy from the Lord is paired with accountability for disobedience, a secondary frame for mercy and judgment.
Details the barrier's iron-and-copper construction immediately before its stated function and eventual collapse.
God's making the earth a barren level surface closely parallels making the barrier dakkā'.
God makes the mountain dakk when He manifests, providing the closest other use of the focus's destruction image.
Places Dhu al-Qarnayn at the people and location whose protection is completed in the focus.
The Book's freedom from crookedness is a broad same-surah theological frame without a direct link to the event.
Joseph calls a prior vision made true by his Lord, supporting the focus's insistence that the Lord's promise is true.
God's empowerment and provision of means explain the capacity behind the barrier later called divine mercy.
The garden parable begins with divine making, but it does not clarify the barrier, mercy, or promise.
Its latter promise brings destruction after wrongdoing, closely paralleling a future promise that makes a constructed state collapse.
The repaired wall anticipates the nearby theme of a protective structure whose hidden divine purpose is later explained.
The Lord's mercy and inability of other gods to save provide only a general theological contrast.
Reward for the righteous does not materially clarify the barrier's mercy, time limit, or promised destruction.
The brief continuation of travel adds no independent understanding beyond the local narrative sequence.
The making of moon and sun has no meaningful relation to the focus's barrier or promise.
Both groups affirm that their Lord's promise proved true, directly reinforcing the focus's final assertion.
Divine mercy creates protection and ease for the youths, a secondary same-surah parallel to the barrier as mercy.
The legal list of prohibited marriages does not clarify the focus.
Explicitly calls God's promise true and joins return with recompense, strongly supporting the focus's certainty of its future fulfilment.
Dhu al-Qarnayn's divinely framed choice of punishment or good treatment develops his role before the barrier episode.
The appointed meeting with the Lord and denial of an appointment support the focus's future-oriented divine promise.
The declaration of a straight path adds no clear relation to mercy, the barrier, or its collapse.
The protected sleepers belong to the same surah's preservation motifs but do not clarify the focus's event.
Repentance and forgiveness give only a broad mercy relation.
It contrasts a claimed personal entitlement to mercy with the coming Hour, sharpening the focus's humble attribution of mercy and certainty of promise.
The local division between punishment for wrongdoing and reward for belief frames Dhu al-Qarnayn's just rule before the mercy of the barrier.
Destroyed towns have an appointed time, providing a secondary parallel to the barrier's divinely fixed end.
Calls God's promise true, though its promised content is enduring reward rather than the barrier's collapse.
Divine guidance and protection in the cave narrative provide a same-surah pattern for mercy as God-given preservation.
The people without shelter provide geographic narrative context but do not illuminate the focus's barrier.
Mercy, resolve, and trust in God form a broad ethical parallel only.
The immediate positive treatment of believers establishes the just, merciful governance that culminates in the barrier episode.
God's forgiveness and mercy are general attributes without a specific event relation.
The coming of fear in a battle description does not clarify the promised destruction in the focus.
A wall preserved for orphans is explicitly called mercy from the Lord, making it a close structural parallel to the barrier called mercy.
The ordered heavens do not add to the focus's mercy, promise, or dakk imagery.
God's making victory a reassurance is a distant parallel to a divinely made protective benefit.
The short notice of resumed travel supplies no independent focus relation.
The believers' calling on the Merciful names the attribute but adds no barrier or promise context.
Divine victory as reassurance is only a remote parallel to the barrier's protective role.
God's acceptance of repentance is a general mercy connection.
The recognition of truth when it comes does not clarify the focus's promise.
The youths ask for mercy and right direction, a same-surah pattern of seeking divine protection.
Past messengers, retribution, and aid to believers provide a broad pattern of divine judgment and support.
A divinely decreed sign and mercy give a secondary parallel to the focus's mercy and certain promise.
It states that the Lord's promise is surely fulfilled, nearly echoing the focus's closing claim.
The single divine name al-Rahman adds only the most general mercy resonance.
The ark's God-dependent movement and the Lord's forgiveness and mercy form a protective-deliverance parallel.
The hypothetical angel made a man does not clarify the focus.
Noah appeals to the truth of God's promise, providing a direct but different narrative use of the formula.
Repentance followed by God's returning mercy supplies a broad contrary response to a fixed destructive outcome.
Abraham's observation of a setting star does not clarify the focus.
The earth's adornment is temporary test material, supporting the focus's declaration that an apparently durable structure will not last.
The Lord neither errs nor forgets offers a distant basis for confidence in His stated promise.
The Merciful Lord delays punishment but assigns an unavoidable appointment, closely framing mercy alongside a fixed future event.
The observation of the moon has no material relation to the focus.
The prayer for forgiveness and mercy is a general attribute-level parallel only.
Abraham's rejection of celestial worship does not clarify the focus.
Mercy precedes life-giving rain and resurrection, a secondary image of divine mercy and future fulfilment.
Explicitly says God will not break His promise, directly reinforcing the focus's final certainty.
Earthly provision and return to God provide only a broad creation-and-return relation.
The unknown nearness or duration of what is promised gives a limited temporal parallel.
The Book is described as guidance and mercy for believers, extending the focus's attribution of mercy to divine provision.
The recipient calls an extraordinary provision a favor from his Lord and a test of gratitude, closely paralleling Dhu al-Qarnayn's attribution rather than self-credit.
God's determination of offspring does not clarify the barrier, promise, or mercy in the focus.
The true Day and return to the Lord provide an eschatological setting for the focus's true promised event.
Entry into God's mercy for believing givers gives only a broad mercy relation.
It rejects despair of the Lord's mercy, clarifying the reach of the mercy named in the focus.
The true speech permitted on the final Day supplies a secondary eschatological context for the focus's truthful promise.
Divine reprieve until a named term and its arrival parallel a mercy-delayed but certain appointed event.
Earthly adornment is suddenly made like a harvested field when God's command comes, strongly paralleling the barrier made dakkā' when the promise comes.
Those in error are extended until they see what they are promised, directly linking deferred time with certain punishment or the Hour.
God's mercy toward believers is general and does not specify the focus's protective event.
The denier is urged to believe because God's promise is true, directly matching the focus's final affirmation in a contrary response.
The Messenger as mercy to the worlds gives a broad, expansive frame for mercy but no specific event relation.
Speaking only the truth from God is a distant support for the focus's truth claim.
God's merciful victory is a remote divine-support parallel.
The speaker's knowledge of deeds adds no material relation to the focus.
The challenge asking when the promise will come supplies a direct contrary posture toward the focus's certain promise.
The prohibition of associating another god does not clarify the barrier or promised collapse.
The polemic against other gods does not materially clarify the focus.
God-given love for believers is a general mercy outcome only.
The Book sent down in truth and the command against doubt offer a secondary epistemic parallel to the focus's claim that the promise is true.
The detailed Book as guidance and mercy for believers extends the focus's attribution of mercy to the Lord.
God's dominance over His affair gives only a broad basis for the focus's certainty that His promise occurs.
Obedience is linked to receiving mercy, supplying a general human response to the mercy named in the focus.
The command to cast Moses' staff does not clarify the focus.
Repentance and faith after wrongdoing are met with forgiveness and mercy, a contrary mercy path alongside the focus's promised destruction.
The immediate continuation releases Gog and Magog, gathers all at the Trumpet, and completes the focus's promised removal of their barrier.
The next ayah presents Hell to the disbelievers, extending the focus's eschatological aftermath.
The removal of mountains, exposure of the earth, and universal gathering closely develop the focus's dakkā' and promised-event horizon.
Its flourishing earthly scene becomes dry debris by God's command, paralleling the transience of the apparently durable barrier.
Mercy remains open, but return brings return of consequence; it supplies a close same-surah pattern of mercy, recurrence, and divine judgment.
God will scatter the mountains, providing a direct counterpart to making the barrier dakkā'.
The land is left a smooth, level plain after the mountains are removed, closely illuminating the result expressed by dakkā'.
The mountains are crushed completely, a direct lexical and eschatological parallel to the focus's dakkā'.
The earth and mountains shake and the mountain becomes a loose sandhill, extending the focus's destruction image.
The mountains are blown away, giving another eschatological counterpart to the focus's removal of a great structure.
The setting in motion of mountains supports the focus's image of a fixed barrier made level at the promised time.
Mountains becoming scattered wool provide a secondary parallel to the focus's dakkā' image.
The direct assertion that God's promise is true nearly repeats the focus's final claim.
God's promise is true, though most people do not know; this directly reinforces the focus's certainty.
It explicitly declares God's promise true and notes human ignorance, closely supporting the focus's closing statement.
God's promise has no alteration, strengthening the focus's assurance of a fixed promised event.
It explicitly states that God does not fail His promise, directly grounding the focus's declaration of truth.
God says He promised the promise of truth, a direct formulation parallel to the focus's true promise.
Those raised from graves recognize what the Merciful promised and affirm the messengers spoke truth, closely joining mercy, promise, and truth.
The deniers' question about when the promise will come supplies a direct contrary response to the focus's certainty.
God's command is coming and must not be hastened, providing a close future-certainty parallel.
When God's command comes, judgment is made in truth; this supports the focus's future promise and its certain execution.
The command to be patient rests on the truth of God's promise, giving a direct confidence-in-promise formulation.
God's promise is true whether its consequence is shown soon or later, clarifying the certainty despite unknown timing.
The acknowledgment that God's promise and the Hour are true supplies an explicit eschatological parallel.
Those who denied are asked whether the promised reality is true and answer yes, reinforcing the focus's assertion.
God gathers people for a day without doubt and does not break His promise, supporting the focus's promised future event.
The prayer relies on God not breaking His promise to the messengers, a direct trust-in-promise counterpart.
God's promise is described as true, though in the distinct context of covenantal reward.
God fulfills His promise to the messengers and saves whom He wills, giving a historical fulfilment pattern.
The recreation of creation is a promise binding on God, adding an eschatological promise-and-fulfilment parallel.
The approaching Hour and split moon give a concentrated sign of the promised eschatological event.
The Day of Decision is an appointed time, supplying temporal certainty for the focus's future promise.
Job's restoration is called mercy from God, a close attribution-of-mercy parallel in a different setting.
A family restoration is explicitly mercy from God, adding another concrete divine mercy attribution.
Solomon identifies a benefit as his Lord's favor and a test, closely paralleling Dhu al-Qarnayn's refusal to claim the barrier as self-made.
God teaches protective armor against violence, providing a secondary parallel to the barrier as divinely enabled protection.
God provides shelters and protective garments, extending the focus's theme of divinely given protection.
